title: Dharma talk with Kanshin Allison Tait at Samish Sesshin
speaker: Kanshin Allison Tait
summary: Kanshin Allison Tait takes up Huineng's Formless Repentance in the Platform Sutra alongside the repentance of the Twelve Steps, then turns to Gateless Barrier case 13, Deshan carrying his bowls. Kanshin opens with Terence's line "Nothing human is alien to me" and Norman Fischer's remark that the problem with San Francisco Zen Center is that everyone there is a human being. Huineng's line "forever to engage in no action is called repentance" meets the GRIP program at San Quentin, where twelve men's 623 years of sentences trace to under two minutes of violence. In case 13, Deshan accepts the Tenzo's rebuke, and Yantou whispers a turning word that changes Deshan's next talk. Kanshin closes by reading a Tiger's Cave passage on crying and laughing with emptiness in the heart.

It was really adorable.

this world with its wars and its pandemics and traffic accidents and cancers.

Seeing all of that and allowing myself to sort of feel it a little bit, I wanted very much to stop creating my own little pieces of unnecessary suffering to throw on top of that heap of suffering already out there in the world.
I think that's what brings many of us to spiritual practice and to 12-step recovery, right?
We get tired of creating unnecessary suffering for ourselves and others, and then we keep doing it anyway, right?
We're already free.
We've always been free.
But habit energy is very strong and craving is very seductive.
So despite being free, we manage to get ourselves tied up and caught again and again and again.
Years ago, when I was still living in Canada, I noticed that I was sort of getting into the same unhealthy relationship over and over again with different partners.
I'm probably the only person who's ever done that.
I thought this relationship was different.
And then I realized, "Oh, no, this is actually the same relationship again."
So I went to my Zen teacher at the time, just so upset and discouraged.
I said, "Why?
Why am I doing this?
Why do I keep hurting myself in this same way over and over again?"
He kind of shrugged and said to me, "I guess you're still getting something out of it," which was the last thing I wanted to hear.
I was so angry at him for saying that.
We don't want to admit it, do we?
Part of the reason we do it over and over again is because we don't know any better.
But once we know better, we're still getting something out of it.
That's why we do it.
It's a really great passage in the meditation and recovery essays that I'm sure Jiriki or Nomon have already talked about, but it's new to me.
It's really good: *We have not once sought to be one in a family, to be a friend among friends, to be a worker among workers, to be a useful member of society.
Always we have tried to struggle to the top of the heap or to hide underneath it.* And I think that kind of attitude was what I was getting out of these relationships, right?
Either I was going to be able to fix them or they would break me.
But either way, I didn't have to worry about living an ordinary life.
So what do we do?
There's no cure for being human, at least not in this lifetime.
But we can't keep going as we are.
So how can we be human in a saner and healthier way?
And I think both the Twelve Steps and the Platform Sutra.
See, I made it.
Both the Twelve Steps and the Platform Sutra agree that it begins with the practice of repentance.
So it's the Platform Sutra of the sixth ancestor, whose name was Huineng.
And Huineng's version of the process of repentance is much shorter than in the Twelve Steps.
This particular section of the Platform Sutra is basically the transcript of a Dharma talk.
So Huineng couldn't go into too much detail, because he had to wrap up before the kitchen crew bowed out.
In Huineng's Formless Repentance, he talked about the formless refuges, the formless repentance and the formless precepts.
For the formless repentance, he says, I will bestow upon you the formless repentance.
Please place your hands in gassho and repeat after me.
*May this disciple be, in past, present, and future thought, in every thought, unstained by delusion.
May delusion be wiped away at once and never arise again.
May this disciple be, in past, present, and future thought, in every thought, unstained by ignorance and arrogance.*
*May ignorance and arrogance be wiped away at once and never arise again.
May this disciple be, in past, present, and future thought, in every thought, unstained by hatred and jealousy.
May hatred and jealousy be wiped away at once and never arise again.*
They did have to repeat it three times, but it's still pretty short.
Of course, when you work the Twelve Steps, it's a much more intensive process involving making a searching and fearless moral inventory, confessing wrongs, making amends to those we have harmed.
And then after doing all that, exhausted and tearful, we find out, oh yeah, that was the preliminary groundwork.
You've finished dealing with the leftover stuff, but now your real work starts.
But don't worry, you have the rest of your life to do it.
For the rest of our lives, we continue to take inventory and promptly admit our wrongs.
That's a whole life's work right there.
*Good friends, what is repentance?
Repentance is to know the mistakes and evil actions you have perpetrated up to now and never let them be absent from the mind.
Repentance is to know the mistakes and evil actions you have perpetrated up to now and never let them be absent from the mind.
And never let them be absent from the mind.
It is useless to make a confession in words before the Buddhas.*
He's bringing some hard truths, isn't he?
And I think we're all grown up enough to hear those truths: that our actions are consequential and irrevocable, and we must never lose sight of that.
A few years ago I did a Buddhist chaplaincy training at the Insight Meditation Centre.
Our class went on a field trip to San Quentin, and we sat in on a meeting of the Guiding Rage Into Power, the GRIP program at San Quentin, which is a program for violent offenders.
I think there's 12 men per cohort.
At the first meeting, the group got together and they added up their collective sentences, how much time everyone's doing.
It was some astronomical number, like 623 years.
As an aside, prison and sentencing reform are really overdue in the U.S., by the way.
So between the 12 of them, they were serving 623 years.
And then they added up all the time collectively they'd spent committing the violent offence that got them imprisoned.
Altogether it was under two minutes, right?
And I think we all know that, hopefully, in less extreme ways.
We've all had that experience, hopefully only metaphorically, of being at the top of the expert ski slope and not listening to that little voice that says, is this a good idea?
Right?
Very quickly we can do an injury to our bodies, our psyche, our relationship that will never heal, right?
One careless word or action.
So I think this is good to remember.
It's good to keep that teaching close.
And then Huineng goes on to say something very peculiar about repentance.
He says, *In my teaching, forever to engage in no action is called repentance.*
*In my teaching, forever to engage in no action is called repentance.* There are several different versions of the Platform Sutra floating around.
In some other versions of it, Huineng says, *forever to engage in no evil action is repentance.* And it's possible the [unclear: "Dan Wang"] manuscript just has a typo.
But let's play it [unclear: "as a lie"], right?
What could Huineng possibly mean by forever to engage in no action?
I think Tim basically summed it up yesterday: "The great way is not difficult.
Simply avoid picking and choosing."
That is to forever engage in no action.
I think my favourite Zen book of all time is The Tiger's Cave, which is a commentary on the Heart Sutra by Abbot Obora, translated by Trevor Leggett.
And there's a wonderful passage about acting from emptiness.
Avoid picking and choosing.
Abbot Obora says:
*My throat is dry.
Consider our life as it is, with its crying and laughing.
There is, in each case, a trace left of crying, and of laughing, the trace of that laughter.
Our living leaves these traces.
The tracks left by grief and joy are footmarks.
In religious terms, a Zen master Dogen calls them the heavy burden of ignorance, the root of evil.
Though I die, the roots of the evil I have created are not annihilated.
When he calls it a load, he means that all the time in our progress through life, there is a great burden which is more than we can really bear.
And shouldering it, we are drenched in sweat until finally our human life ends.
We long somehow to put it down, by some means to lighten ourselves of the weight of conceptual thinking.
But to do so, we have to be earnest seekers.*
*If we are not, there is no religion.
The quest for inner lightness, to be able to cry, but with an emptiness within the heart.
To laugh, but with the same emptiness.
Such is the great wisdom.
To do things with an inner emptiness is the wisdom of the knowledge of ultimate emptiness.
The power of negating into emptiness is the great wisdom.*
And then he talks about the Heart Sutra as a lecture given by Kenan Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion.
So, [unclear: "Abhidhabhura"] speaks of this.

We wretched human beings do not do that.
On our lips are congratulations, but in our heart, kushu.
We have no freedom of sound, no spontaneity in our words.
Holy Kenan always has emptiness in the heart, whether in joy or in sorrow, and so he has freedom of mind.
It is the power of ultimate emptiness.
In the negative sense, it is emptiness.
But in the positive sense, it means that in our crying or laughing, body and mind are one.
This is the true spontaneity of speech.
When our words are directed to freeing others and freeing ourselves, the grace of Kenan Bodhisattva will be in that place.*
We studied the Song of the Jyotmira Samadhi last year.

And Abbot Sekhita, who did a really lovely commentary on the Gateless Barrier and the Book of Serenity, said that the ultimate example of acting from emptiness is a particular koan, case 13 of the Gateless Barrier.
I didn't bring this up when I was teaching the class on the Song of the Jyotmira Samadhi because I didn't understand this koan at all.
And nobody called me out on it.
Until now.
But case 13 of the Gateless Barrier: Taishan carries his bowls.
It's about a teacher showing up for the meal at the wrong time.
I was planning to talk about this anyway, but then yesterday evening when I got out of Dokusan, I had the schedule wrong in my head.
I thought service started at 5:45.
So I checked the time, and I thought, oh, I'll be just a little bit late for service when I walk to the Zendo.
And nobody was here.
Everybody was already in the dining room.
By the time I made it back to the dining room from the Zendo, you'd already started eating.
So I didn't want to barge in and interrupt.
I went to my cabin to work on this talk.
And then after a few minutes, I started feeling hungry.
So I thought, well, if I time it right, maybe I can show up after they've finished eating, but before they put the leftovers away, and the Tenzo will give me something.
And the Tenzo did, fortunately, but I didn't time it right.
I showed up while everyone was still cleaning their bowls, and I stood there like a doofus for about ten minutes.
I didn't get enlightened, though.
So, enough about me.
In case 13 of the Mumonkan, it's Teishon who's the doofus.
He was early, though.
So the story goes: Abbot Teishon shows up in the dining room carrying his bowls.
And the Tenzo says, rather rudely, "They haven't played the meal drum yet.
Where are you going with your bowl?"
At those words Teishon turned around and meekly returned to his cabin.
Now, this is notable because up until then, Teishon was known for having a fiery temper.
So for him to accept correction so quietly was a little bit strange.
Another monk, a good friend of Teishon's, Yando, heard about this.
And he said in response, "I think that old monk almost has it now after all these years."
He said that to someone else, to the Tenzo, actually.
But he said it to the Tenzo knowing that the Abbot would hear about it.
And sure enough, Teishon pulled him aside a little bit later and said, "What do you mean, almost?"
In response, Yando leaned in and whispered something into Teishon's ear.
We don't know what.
It doesn't say.
It was something very important.
It was a turning word that Yando had wanted to share with his friend Teishon, but hadn't been able to, because Teishon's temper kept him at bay.
Teishon's temper would have kept him from hearing it.
At this moment, after seeing how he carried his bowls to the dining room and then back to his cabin, Yando said, "I think it's time.
It's time for me to say this thing that he really needs to hear."
Which makes me wonder: what do my good friends know about me that I'm still too neurotic to hear?
It gives me a good reason to keep practicing, right?
Waiting for the day when an old monk can whisper in my ear what I really need to get past whatever mental block I've set upon myself.
Because this is what happened with Yando and Teishon.
The next day, they said, Teishon gave a Dharma talk, and it was completely unlike any Dharma talk he'd ever given before.
Nobody could understand the change in him.
He suddenly was able to step forward as a teacher, a teacher his old friend Yando had always known he could be.
Hearing that, Yando clapped his hands and shouted, "He's really caught it.
He understands the whole thing."
And by the way, many, many years later, Yando was also able to offer a turning word to the Tenzo to help get him over his own mental roadblock, which was different from Teishon's, but also difficult.
I want to end by repeating that section from the Tiger's Cave.
*The tracks left by joy or grief are footmarks.
In religious terms, Dogen calls them the heavy burden of ignorance, the root of evil.
Though I die, the roots of the evil I have created are not annihilated.
When he calls it a load, he means that all the time in our progress through life, there is a great burden, which is more than we can really bear.
In shouldering it, we are drenched in sweat until finally our human life ends.
We long somehow to put it down, by some means to lighten ourselves of the weight of conceptual thinking.
But to do so, we have to be earnest seekers.
If we are not, there is no religion.
The quest for inner lightness, to be able to cry, but with an emptiness within the heart, to laugh but with the same emptiness, such is the great wisdom.
To do things with an inner emptiness is the wisdom of the knowledge of ultimate emptiness.
This is the great wisdom.*
Thank you all very much for your kind attention.
Please take very good care of yourselves.
